# DeRot blog: full text

# Why Does Scrolling Make Me Anxious? What Your Body Is Reacting To

URL: https://derot.org/blog/why-does-scrolling-make-me-anxious/
Updated: 2026-10-28

Key takeaways:
- Scrolling can make you anxious because the feed stacks threat-heavy news, social comparison, rapid switching and unresolved stories, often while you sit hunched with short, shallow breaths.
- In 2021 experiments, just 2 to 4 minutes of COVID-19 news lowered positive mood (an effect size of about 0.4), while stories about kindness did not.
- What you see and how you scroll (passive watching versus active use) appear to matter at least as much as total minutes.
- Most research linking scrolling and anxiety is correlational, the effects are modest, and the link may run both ways: anxious people may also scroll more.
- A mid-scroll reset of five slow breaths (inhale 4, exhale 6, about 50 seconds) or one to three physiological sighs can help you feel calmer.

Scrolling can make you anxious because the feed mixes threat-flavored news, social comparison, rapid switching and stories that never resolve, and that mix can keep your body braced. A hunched posture and shallow breathing can add to it. Research shows associations and short-term mood dips, not proof that scrolling causes anxiety, and what you see matters more than minutes alone.

That last point is the one we keep coming back to at DeRot. The problem usually isn't you, and it isn't only the number on your screen time report. It's the state the feed leaves you in. Below we cover what that state feels like, the likeliest reasons it happens, what the evidence does and doesn't support, and a reset you can use in the middle of the feed, right when you notice it, in under a minute.

## What scroll anxiety feels like in your body

Scroll anxiety usually shows up in the body before it shows up as a thought: a tight jaw, shoulders creeping toward your ears, short breaths high in the chest, and a buzzy, wired-but-tired feeling. Many people only notice it when they finally look up.

The classic version goes like this. You pick up your phone to check one message. Twenty minutes later you surface, and something has shifted. Nothing bad actually happened to you. You read a few headlines, watched some clips, saw a friend's holiday photos. Yet your teeth are pressed together, your neck aches, and there's a low hum of dread you can't quite place.

Sensations people commonly describe:

- A clenched jaw, or the tongue pressed hard against the roof of the mouth
- Shoulders raised and rounded forward
- Quick, shallow breathing up in the chest, sometimes with small unnoticed breath holds
- A tight chest, or a heart that feels like it's going faster than it should
- Restlessness: wanting to keep scrolling and wanting to stop, at the same time
- Feeling tired and switched on at once

The confusing part is that scrolling is often what people reach for to relax. So when they come out of it feeling worse, they assume something is wrong with them. More often, the body is doing something reasonable: reacting to a steady stream of small alarms, comparisons and unfinished stories as if they mattered, because some of them might.

### Why does my heart race while scrolling?

A racing heart while scrolling is a common way of feeling keyed up, as if your body is getting ready for something that never arrives. We're not aware of any study that has measured heart rate during ordinary everyday scrolling, so we won't put numbers on it. What we can say is that a braced body and fast, shallow breathing tend to travel together, and the sense of a pounding heart often comes along with them. If it happens often, comes with chest pain, or shows up away from your phone too, get it checked by a doctor.

## Why does scrolling make me anxious? Six likely contributors

Scrolling can make you anxious because several things stack up at once: threat-heavy content, comparison, constant switching, rewards you can't predict, stories with no ending, and a cramped posture. Some of these have experimental support. Others are plausible explanations that haven't been tested directly in scrolling. We'll say which is which.

### 1. Threat-flavored news lowers your mood fast

Brief exposure to negative news measurably dents mood. In a 2021 set of experiments, [about two minutes of COVID-19 news on Twitter lowered positive affect in a study of 299 people](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8513826/), with an effect size of d = 0.42. In a second study of 603 people, about four minutes of COVID news on YouTube lowered positive affect (d = 0.40) and optimism (d = 0.28).

Two details matter. First, those are small-to-moderate effects from very short doses, likely shorter than many scroll sessions. Second, negative affect did not rise significantly. What dropped was the good stuff. That fits how a lot of people describe the comedown: less outright panic, more flat, braced and vaguely uneasy.

### 2. Upward comparison during passive scrolling

Watching other people's highlights without interacting is linked to feeling worse, and envy seems to be the route. A 2015 paper combining a lab experiment and a field study found that [passive Facebook use lowered affective well-being over time, through increased envy](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25706656/), while active use did not. In the field part, researchers [texted about 80 undergraduates five times a day for six days](https://news.umich.edu/passive-facebook-use-undermines-how-a-person-feels) to track how they felt as they used the site.

A 2021 review in World Psychiatry concluded that [damaging social comparisons drive much of the harm in passive use](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801842). Envy isn't the same as anxiety, but it's a close relative: the sense of falling behind, which the body tends to treat as something to keep an eye on.

### 3. Rapid switching between unrelated content

The feed asks you to change emotional gears every few seconds: a war headline, a puppy, an ad, a friend's engagement, a cooking hack, a stranger's argument. In a study of 318 adults, [higher media multitasking was associated with more symptoms of depression and social anxiety](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23126438/), even after accounting for total media use and personality.

That's an association only. It doesn't show that switching causes anxiety. But it's one of the few findings that points at how you consume rather than how much, and it matches the scattered feeling many people have after a long session.

### 4. "Maybe the next post" keeps you braced

Feeds deliver something genuinely interesting at unpredictable intervals. A plausible explanation for the wired feeling is that not knowing when the good post will appear keeps you in a mild state of anticipation: thumb ready, attention pitched forward. You'll often see this described online as a "dopamine loop," which overstates what is actually known about brain chemistry during scrolling. The simpler version is enough. Uncertainty tends to keep people alert, and alert is not the same as relaxed.

### 5. Stories that never resolve

Very little in a feed ends. You see the start of a crisis, a heated thread, a teaser for a video, then the next thing. Another plausible contributor is this pile-up of open loops: half-finished stories your mind keeps holding after your thumb has moved on. There isn't direct research on this in scrolling, so treat it as a reasonable idea rather than a finding. It does explain why the dread can feel vague. It isn't about one thing. It's about twenty unfinished things.

### 6. Slumped posture and shallow breathing

How you hold your body while you scroll may play a part. In a small randomized study, [one hour of seated smartphone use (participants were playing a game) reduced forced vital capacity from 3.2 to 3.0 liters and forced expiratory volume in one second from 3.0 to 2.7 liters](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4905897/) compared with controls. Another small, cross-sectional study found that [head and shoulder posture and peak expiratory flow differed by how long people used their smartphones](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/28/1/28_jpts-2015-817/_article).

These are small, short-term studies (in the first, the two groups weren't evenly matched at the start), and lung function isn't the same thing as anxiety. Still, they line up with what many people feel: curled over the phone, chest compressed, breath sitting high and short. A body breathing like that can feel more on edge. If you want the bigger picture of how all of this builds up, our guide to [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/) goes deeper.

## Is it the time you spend or what you're looking at?

What you see and how you scroll appear to matter at least as much as total minutes. The same experiments that showed doom-scrolling dents mood found that kindness-scrolling did not, and other research separates passive watching from active use.

Back to those 2021 experiments: participants who watched [stories about acts of kindness did not show the drop in mood](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8513826/) seen in those who watched COVID news. Same platforms, similar time, different content, different result.

The 2021 review draws a similar line around how you use social media: [passive use is linked to declining well-being over time, while active use is not](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801842). In plain terms, silently watching other people's lives seems to land differently from talking with them.

Time still matters somewhat. In a 2018 University of Pennsylvania experiment, [143 students who limited social media to about 30 minutes a day (10 minutes per platform) for three weeks reported less depression and loneliness](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/11/181108164316.htm) than a control group. Nobody was asked to quit: the limit was 10 minutes per platform. Note that the clearest results were for depression and loneliness, not anxiety.

That detail is worth sitting with. Cutting back, rather than cutting out, was enough to make a difference for these students, so quitting isn't the only lever. It's also a reminder that one small study of students can't settle the question for everyone.

This is why we think in terms of state over quantity. Twenty minutes of messages with friends and good-news stories can leave you fine. Five minutes of grim headlines can leave you wound up. If you want practical ways to change the mix without giving up your phone, see [how to stop doomscrolling without quitting your phone](/blog/how-to-stop-doomscrolling/).

## What the research does and doesn't show

The honest summary: links between scrolling and anxiety are real but mostly correlational, the experimental effects are modest and short-term, and the relationship may run in both directions.

Here's what that means in practice:

- **Mostly correlational.** [Among 800 students in Iran and the US, a stronger tendency to doomscroll was associated with higher existential anxiety](https://news.flinders.edu.au/blog/2024/07/18/can-doomscrolling-trigger-an-existential-crisis/), a finding also summarized by the [BPS Research Digest](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/creeping-influence-doomscrolling). The media multitasking study above is correlational too. Studies like these can't tell us what causes what.
- **Direction unclear.** Coverage of other doomscrolling research notes that [the direction of cause between doomscrolling and anxiety is unclear](https://www.weforum.org/stories/2022/01/doomscrolling-behavior-social-media/). Anxious people may reach for the feed more, looking for reassurance, information or distraction.
- **Possibly two-way.** The 2021 review describes the overall link between social media use and well-being as [negative but small, and possibly reciprocal](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801842).
- **Short-term, modest effects.** The doom-scrolling experiments measured mood right after a few minutes of exposure. Effect sizes around 0.4 are meaningful but not dramatic, and those studies didn't follow people over weeks.
- **Narrow samples.** Much of this work uses students and young adults, so it may not map neatly onto everyone.

None of this means your experience isn't real. It means the feeling you notice after a scroll is a reasonable thing to pay attention to, and probably a better guide than headlines claiming the feed is rewiring your brain. You don't need a diagnosis to decide you'd like to come out of the app feeling better than you went in.

## A 60-second reset to use mid-scroll

The most useful moment to calm down is the one where you notice you're wound up, which is usually mid-scroll, not before you open the app. Five slow breaths with a longer exhale, or one to three physiological sighs, take under a minute and can help you feel calmer.

Why mid-scroll? Because that's when the jaw is tight and the breath is high. A rule you set before opening an app doesn't meet you there, and you can't regulate a feeling you haven't had yet. You don't have to close the app or make any big decisions. Just pause.

Start with a five-second setup: put the phone down on your lap or the table, sit back or straighten up a little, let your shoulders drop, and unclench your jaw.

### Script A: five long-exhale breaths (about 50 seconds)

1. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4.
2. Breathe out slowly through your nose or softly pursed lips for a count of 6.
3. Keep the exhale smooth and unhurried, like fogging a window from a distance.
4. Repeat for five breaths. That's about 50 seconds.
5. Check where your shoulders and jaw are now, then go back to the app or put the phone away.

Each breath takes 10 seconds, so this works out to about six breaths a minute. That sits inside what a 2018 systematic review defined as slow breathing, [under 10 breaths per minute](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6137615/), which across 15 studies was associated with higher heart rate variability and better emotional control in healthy adults. The review is clear that the evidence base is small, so think of this as a promising, low-risk practice rather than a proven fix.

For a fuller walkthrough, see our [4-6 breathing guide](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/), or follow the free [calm breathing 4-6 timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) so you don't have to count.

### Script B: one to three physiological sighs (about 15 to 30 seconds)

1. Breathe in through your nose until you feel comfortably full.
2. Without breathing out, take a second, shorter sip of air through your nose to top up.
3. Breathe out slowly through your mouth, all the way, letting it take longer than both inhales together.
4. Take one or two ordinary breaths.
5. Repeat once or twice more if it helps. Stop at three.

The research here is a 2023 randomized trial of 108 people, in which [five minutes a day of cyclic sighing for 28 days produced the largest rise in positive mood](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/) among the techniques tested. State anxiety fell about equally in every group, including mindfulness meditation, and the authors described the work as exploratory. Using one to three sighs in the moment goes beyond what was studied, so treat it as a sensible adaptation rather than a tested protocol. The free [physiological sigh timer](/tools/physiological-sigh/) paces it for you.

### What it should feel like

Done gently, you'll usually feel your shoulders slide down, your jaw loosen and the exhale start to lengthen on its own. Some people notice a small yawn or a softening across the chest. You're not aiming for bliss. You're aiming for one notch down from wired.

### Common mistakes

- **Oversized breaths.** Big gulps can make you lightheaded. Aim for comfortable, not maximal.
- **Lifting the shoulders to breathe in.** Let the belly and lower ribs move instead.
- **Rushing the exhale.** The slow out-breath is the point of the exercise. If 6 counts feels like a strain, try inhale 3, exhale 5.
- **Doing one breath and judging it.** One breath rarely changes much. Five usually does more.

If you'd rather not have to remember any of this in the moment, that's the reason we built DeRot: it pauses your scroll to bring you back down with a few calming breaths, then lets you carry on. It's coming soon to iOS.

### Safety notes

- Keep breaths gentle. If you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly, stop and breathe normally.
- Physiological sighs are one to three in a row, not dozens. Don't use breath holds or fast breathing as your reset.
- If you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, have a history of fainting, or find that focusing on your breath makes panic worse, go gently or check with a clinician first. The 2023 sighing trial excluded similar groups.

## Why scrolling at night can feel worse

Scrolling at night can feel worse because your body is trying to wind down while the feed keeps handing it things to react to. Unresolved stories and late headlines have nowhere to go when you're lying in the dark.

During the day, other things dilute the feed: conversations, errands, work, movement. At night there's less of that. A heated thread or a worrying headline can be the last thing you take in before trying to sleep, and the open loops from earlier have a quiet room to echo in. Lying curled up with the phone close to your face may not help your breathing either.

The same reset works here. Try five breaths of 4-6 with the phone face down on your chest before you decide whether to keep going. For more on why the nighttime version feels so wired, read [doomscrolling at night and a way back down](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/).

## When it's more than the feed

If the anxious feeling sticks around after you put the phone down, it may be about more than scrolling, and it's worth talking to someone.

Consider reaching out to a GP or a mental health professional if:

- The anxiety lasts long after you've stopped scrolling
- It shows up most days
- It's disrupting your sleep, work or relationships
- It comes with panic attacks, or a racing heart and tight chest that happen away from your phone

A professional can talk you through options, which commonly include talking therapies such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). You don't have to wait until things feel serious to ask.

If you or someone you know may be in crisis, call or text 988 in the US, or contact your local emergency services.

Breathing exercises can help you feel calmer in the moment. They don't treat anxiety disorders, and they aren't a substitute for care. Think of the mid-scroll reset as a way to come down from the feed, not a way to carry something bigger on your own.

## FAQ
**Is it normal to feel anxious after social media?**
Yes, it's a common experience. In experiments, just a few minutes of negative news lowered people's positive mood, so feeling flat, uneasy or wired after a scroll is an understandable response to the content, not a personal failing. It tends to fade once you step away. If it lingers after you put the phone down, shows up most days or affects sleep or work, it's worth talking to a GP or mental health professional.

**Why can't I stop scrolling even though it makes me feel bad?**
Feeds have no natural stopping point and deliver interesting posts at unpredictable moments, so there's always a reason to see one more. When you're already wound up, stopping takes a decision your tense body isn't in the mood to make. A short breathing pause can help because it creates a break without asking you to quit, and once you've come down a little, deciding what to do next usually feels easier.

**Does looking down at my phone affect my breathing?**
Small studies suggest it might. In one small randomized study, an hour of seated smartphone use slightly reduced lung function measures compared with controls, and another linked longer phone use to differences in posture and breathing flow. These studies are small and short-term, so treat them as a reason to sit up and drop your shoulders now and then, not as a cause for worry.

**Should I quit social media to stop feeling anxious?**
Not necessarily. In a 2018 experiment, students who limited social media to about 30 minutes a day for three weeks reported less depression and loneliness, and nobody was asked to quit: cutting back was enough. Changing what you look at, scrolling less passively and resetting when you notice tension are reasonable first steps before anything drastic.

**What can I do right now when scrolling makes me anxious?**
Put the phone down, let your shoulders drop and unclench your jaw. Then take five slow breaths: in through your nose for 4, out slowly for 6. That's about 50 seconds. Or try one to three physiological sighs: two inhales through the nose, then one long exhale through the mouth. Keep it gentle, and stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.

# Screen Time Apps That Aren't Blockers: Gentle Options, Compared

URL: https://derot.org/blog/screen-time-app-not-blocker/
Updated: 2026-10-27

Key takeaways:
- The gentlest iPhone options are one sec, ScreenZen, Inscreen, Jomo and Apple's Screen Time used as a soft reminder, though most also have optional strict modes.
- A delay app adds a pause before an app opens and always lets you continue. A blocker stops access for a set time or on a schedule.
- In a small 42-person Android study, 62% of people kept gentle interventions switched on, compared with 36% for a timed lockout.
- Google's Pause Point is Android-only. On iPhone, one sec and ScreenZen offer the closest thing: a short pause with a breath in it when an app opens.
- Most pauses step in when you open an app. For the wired feeling 20 minutes into a scroll, a minute of slow 4-6 breathing may help you feel calmer.

The best screen time apps that aren't blockers are one sec (a short delay and breath before an app opens), ScreenZen (free, highly configurable delays and check-ins), Inscreen (CBT-style awareness alerts), Jomo (schedules with mindful breaks) and Apple's built-in Screen Time used as a soft reminder. Most also include optional strict modes, so set them up gently.

Set up gently, each pick below is a screen time app that isn't a blocker: it nudges you, delays you or shows you your habits rather than shutting you out. Disclosure: DeRot makes an app in this category. We do not rank our own app, and no app paid to be included. Our app stays out of the table and the list, and it gets one short, labeled section near the end.

## Gentle screen time apps compared at a glance

All prices are in US dollars as shown on each app's US App Store listing, checked October 27, 2026. We include Opal only to show what a strict app looks like. It is not one of our picks.

| App | Best for | How it steps in | What the pause asks of you | Free option | Price (as listed, USD, checked Oct 27, 2026) | Platforms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| one sec | A breath before opening | Delay when an app opens; can step in again after a set time | Watch a breathing animation (via Shortcuts), then choose | Free for 1 app | Pro $6.99/month, $19.99/year or $99.99 lifetime | iOS 15+, macOS 14+ |
| ScreenZen | Free, highly configurable friction | Delay when an app opens that can grow with each open, plus scrolling check-ins | Breathe during the wait; "Is this important?" | Fully free | Free; optional tips of $5, $10, $20 or $40 | iOS 16.4+, macOS 13+, visionOS |
| Inscreen | Reflection over waiting | Scheduled awareness alerts | Ask yourself whether you're on your phone on purpose | Financial-aid free year; free tier not stated | $1.99/month, $14.99/year or $29.99 lifetime | iPhone only, iOS 17.6+ |
| Jomo | Schedules with an escape hatch | Scheduled blocks, caps on opens, mindful breaks | Take a planned break inside your own rules | Not stated | $5.99/month, $29.99/year, $99.99 one-time (also lists $84.99 lifetime) | iOS 16+, macOS 13+ |
| Apple Screen Time | No cost, no new app | Time allowances by category, schedules | A limit screen you can dismiss by default | Built in | Free | iPhone, iPad |
| Opal (strict contrast) | Hard lockouts | Deep Focus sessions that can't be cancelled; gentler Breaks | Breaks: write an intention and set a timer | Not stated | Weekly $4.99 or $9.99, monthly $19.99, yearly $99.99; Pro $49.99 (billing period not stated) | iPhone only, iOS 18+ |

## Delay app vs app blocker: what's the difference?

A delay app (also called a friction app) adds a short pause before a distracting app opens, and you can always continue after it. An app blocker stops access for a set time or on a schedule, and it is designed so that getting in is hard.

Most "mindful" apps sit somewhere between the two. They start out gentle and offer strict options if you want them. ScreenZen offers [optional strict blocks and lock settings](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screenzen-screen-time-control/id1541027222), and its App Store subtitle even calls it an "App blocker." Jomo has a [Strict Mode that locks your rules for a few days by default](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/jomo-screen-time-blocker/id1609960918). Inscreen offers [optional focus blocks and strict limits](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screen-time-control-inscreen/id6737131495).

So in practice, "not a blocker" usually means "not a blocker unless you turn that part on." That matters, because the settings you start with tend to be the ones you keep.

Why choose gentle at all? The best independent evidence we found is small but useful. University of Michigan researchers tested an Android tool called InteractOut with [42 people over five weeks. Gentle friction was about 16% more effective than a timed lockout, and 62% of people kept the gentle interventions switched on, compared with 36% for the lockout](https://www.futurity.org/?p=3224202). It was one small Android study, and it measured phone use rather than how anyone felt, so read it as a hint rather than a verdict.

The hint fits a familiar pattern: a nudge you keep does more than a wall you switch off on day five.

## How we compared

We compared each app on five things:

1. **When and how it steps in:** when you open the app, on a schedule, through limits, or partway through a session.
2. **How strict it can get,** and whether strict mode is optional or the default.
3. **What the pause asks of you:** a breath, a reflection, an intention, or just a wait. This is our "after-feel" criterion. A pause that helps you settle is different from one that only makes you wait, which can leave you more irritated than before. We judge this from listed features only, not from any claims about results.
4. **Price as listed,** in US dollars with the billing period.
5. **Platforms** and minimum iOS version.

Every app fact comes from that app's US App Store listing, checked October 27, 2026. We didn't give star ratings or scores, and we didn't run our own usage trials. Prices and features change, so check the listing before you subscribe.

## Screen time apps that aren't blockers, sorted by how they step in

### Friction at launch: one sec

**Best for:** people who want one deliberate breath between the urge to open an app and the feed itself.

**How it works:** one sec's listing says it [delays access to distracting apps instead of blocking them completely](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/one-sec-screen-time-focus/id1532875441). When you open a chosen app, it can show a breathing animation (it runs through Apple's Shortcuts, which the app now sets up for you), and then you can continue or back out. It can also step in again after you've been in the app for a set time.

**What stands out:** it has more published research behind it than any other app here. In a [six-week field experiment with 280 people, one sec cut actual app openings by 57%, and about 36% of attempts to open an app ended with the person closing it](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9974409). Being offered a way to back out seemed to do most of the work. The delay helped but added little on top, and a message asking people to think it over did not help. Two caveats: the authors include one sec's developer, and these figures come from the paper's abstract.

**Drawbacks:** people get used to friction. A [longer study of 1,039 one sec users over about 13.4 weeks](https://mcml.ai/publications/hgr+24/) found that the frictions did reduce attempts to open apps, but users took breaks from them and quickly went back to heavy use. The free version also covers only one app.

**Price:** free for one app. Pro is [$6.99/month, $19.99/year or $99.99 lifetime](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/one-sec-screen-time-focus/id1532875441), and Family plans are listed too. iOS 15+ and macOS 14+.

### Friction plus check-ins: ScreenZen

**Best for:** anyone who wants a free, highly configurable delay with no subscription.

**How it works:** ScreenZen adds a [delay before an app opens that can get longer with each open, and you can breathe during the wait](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screenzen-screen-time-control/id1541027222). It can also interrupt your scrolling with check-ins and show "Is this important?" style messages.

**What stands out:** the price. It's free, and the only in-app purchases are optional tips. The growing delay is a smart touch: your third open of the hour asks a little more of you than your first.

**Drawbacks:** it isn't purely gentle. The listing includes [optional strict blocks and lock settings, and the subtitle calls it an "App blocker"](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screenzen-screen-time-control/id1541027222). With that many settings, it's easy to end up with something stricter than you meant to set up.

**Price:** free, with optional tips of [$5, $10, $20 or $40](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screenzen-screen-time-control/id1541027222). iOS 16.4+, macOS 13+ and visionOS.

### Awareness prompts: Inscreen

**Best for:** people who'd rather be asked a good question than be made to wait.

**How it works:** Inscreen says it [draws on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) instead of blocking access](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screen-time-control-inscreen/id6737131495). It sends scheduled alerts that ask whether you're using your phone on purpose.

**What stands out:** because the alerts are scheduled, they can reach you partway through a session, not only when you open an app. The question is about intent, not minutes. The listing also offers a financial-aid option for a free year.

**Drawbacks:** it's iPhone only and needs iOS 17.6+. A question is easy to swipe away when you're deep in a feed. It also offers [optional focus blocks and strict limits](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screen-time-control-inscreen/id6737131495) if you want firmer rules. "Draws on CBT" describes how the app is designed. It isn't therapy, and we didn't find published research on the app itself.

**Price:** the Individual plan is [$1.99/month, $14.99/year or $29.99 lifetime](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/screen-time-control-inscreen/id6737131495), and Family plans are listed separately. The listing doesn't state a free tier.

### Soft limits and breaks: Jomo

**Best for:** people who like routines and want scheduled boundaries with a built-in way out.

**How it works:** Jomo is built around schedules. You set [blocks for certain times, with "mindful breaks" to step out of them, plus Locks that cap how many times you can open an app](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/jomo-screen-time-blocker/id1609960918).

**What stands out:** mindful breaks give you a planned exit, so a schedule feels less like a wall. It suits someone who wants structure, like no Instagram during work hours, without being shut out completely.

**Drawbacks:** it leans stricter than the other gentle picks. [Strict Mode locks your rules for a few days by default](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/jomo-screen-time-blocker/id1609960918), so read that setting carefully. The listing also contradicts itself on price.

**Price:** the listing shows [$5.99/month, $29.99/year and $99.99 one-time, and separately lists an $84.99 lifetime option](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/jomo-screen-time-blocker/id1609960918). We can't tell which lifetime price is current, so check in the app before you pay. iOS 16+ and macOS 13+.

### Built in: Apple Screen Time used gently

**Best for:** zero cost and no new app.

**How it works:** Screen Time lets you [set time allowances by app category and a daily budget, and schedule downtime for weekday and weekend routines](https://support.apple.com/en-lamr/108806). Apple has renamed features over the years, so the menu names on your iOS version may differ.

**What stands out:** it's already on your phone. According to one third-party guide, [you can ignore limits by default once you reach them, and Downtime warns you five minutes before it starts](https://www.itechguides.com/use-screen-time-to-cut-app-use-on-iphone-ios-27/). As a wall, that's a weakness. As a soft reminder, it's a decent nudge: a screen telling you that you've spent 30 minutes in an app is useful information, and you can act on it or not.

**Drawbacks:** the limit screen asks nothing of your body or your attention, so you can dismiss it on autopilot. It has roughly the persuasive power of a cookie banner.

**Price:** free, built into iPhone and iPad.

To use it gently, set limits a little above your typical use rather than far below it, skip the Screen Time passcode, and treat the limit screen as a check-in rather than a verdict.

### Strict contrast: Opal

**Best for:** people who actually want a hard lockout.

**How it works:** Opal's Deep Focus sessions are strict by design. The listing says Deep Focus [won't let you cancel or bypass at all](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/opal-screen-time-control/id1497465230). Its gentler feature, Breaks, asks you to write an intention and set a timer before you get in.

**What stands out:** if you only use Breaks, it works as a reasonable tool for setting intentions. We include it so you can see where the line between gentle and strict sits.

**Drawbacks:** the strict features are the core of the product. iPhone only, iOS 18+.

**Price:** the listing shows [weekly plans at $4.99 and $9.99, $19.99 monthly, $99.99 yearly, and a Pro option at $49.99 with no billing period stated](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/opal-screen-time-control/id1497465230).

## Is there an iPhone version of Google's Pause Point?

No, not from Apple. Pause Point is an Android Digital Wellbeing feature that Google [announced at Google I/O on May 12, 2026](https://www.androidauthority.com/pause-point-for-android-3664886/), and the coverage we found says nothing about an iPhone version.

When you open an app you've marked as distracting, Pause Point adds a 10-second pause that asks why you're there. From the pause, you can breathe, look at your photos, set a timer, or switch to another app. To turn the feature off, you have to restart your phone, so switching it off becomes a decision rather than a reflex.

The closest iPhone options are third-party apps:

- **one sec** shows a breathing animation when you open an app, set up through Shortcuts.
- **ScreenZen** adds a delay with breathing during the wait, and the delay grows if you keep reopening the app.

Neither one copies Pause Point exactly. Both give you the same core move: a short pause with a breath in it, which you can always get past.

## Which should you pick?

- If you want a breath before opening an app, pick **one sec**.
- If you want something free and highly configurable, pick **ScreenZen**.
- If you want reflection prompts more than pauses, pick **Inscreen**.
- If you want schedules with a way out, pick **Jomo**, and leave Strict Mode off.
- If you want zero cost and no new app, set **gentle Screen Time limits** a little above your usual use.
- If you want a hard lockout you can't get around, pick a blocker like **Opal's Deep Focus**. Gentle apps aren't built for that, and that's fine.

Whichever you pick, start with the gentlest setting. You can always tighten it later, and the research above suggests that a setting you keep switched on beats one you abandon. For more ways to cut back without giving up your phone, see [how to stop doomscrolling without quitting your phone](/blog/how-to-stop-doomscrolling/).

## What about the moment you're already mid-scroll?

Most of the pauses above step in when you open an app, before the feed has done anything to you. ScreenZen's scrolling check-ins and Inscreen's alerts can arrive mid-session, but they ask about time or intent. None of these apps is built around how you feel 20 minutes in, when your jaw is tight and you feel vaguely wired.

That feeling is real, even though the research is still catching up. In University of Michigan experience-sampling research, which texted people five times a day for two weeks, [passive Facebook scrolling was linked to envy, and that envy predicted drops in how good people felt](https://prod.lsa.umich.edu/psych/news-events/all-news/faculty-news/the-age-of-envy--how-to-be-happy-when-everyone-else-s-life-looks0.html). The evidence is modest, mostly about Facebook and based on self-report, but it matches what many people notice: the feed can leave you feeling worse. The problem is the feed, not you. We go deeper on this in [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/).

Slow breathing is one of the simplest ways to come back down. A [systematic review of 15 studies found that breathing slower than 10 breaths per minute was associated with higher heart rate variability, more relaxation and less arousal](https://ricerca.unich.it/handle/11564/773399), although the evidence base is small. In a [108-person randomized trial, five minutes a day of cyclic sighing (a breathing pattern with long exhales) improved positive mood more than mindfulness meditation over 28 days](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/). But anxiety dropped in every group, with no difference between them, and about 10% of participants reported a negative experience. So the results are promising, not settled.

### A 60-second mid-scroll script

1. Notice the signs: a tight jaw, raised shoulders, a thumb moving faster than you're reading.
2. Put the phone face down.
3. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4.
4. Breathe out slowly for a count of 6.
5. Repeat 5 to 6 times. That takes about a minute, at roughly six breaths per minute.
6. Then decide whether to keep scrolling or close the app. Either is fine. The point is that you chose.

If you'd like something to pace you, use our free [calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) or the [physiological sigh guide](/tools/physiological-sigh/). For the full technique, see [4-6 breathing in 60 seconds](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/).

A quick safety note: stop if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly, and go back to breathing normally. The 4-6 pattern has no breath hold. Patterns that do (box breathing, 4-7-8) and fast breathing aren't for everyone. Take care if you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic, and shorten the counts rather than strain. Breathing can help you feel calmer, but it isn't a treatment. If anxiety, sleep problems or distress keep coming back, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, call 988 in the US or your local emergency number.

## Where DeRot fits (our app)

This is the gap we built our app for. DeRot pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths. It meets you mid-scroll, after the feed has wound you up, instead of standing in front of the app as a gate.

The goal is the comedown: your shoulders drop, your head clears and the wired feeling fades. Spending less time in the feed often follows, but that's a side effect, not the main point. Each reset takes 30 seconds. Calm breathing (in 4, out 6) is the default, Box and 4-7-8 are also included, and Pro unlocks custom patterns. You can always get past the pause by breathing through it.

It isn't for everyone. If you want a hard lockout you can't get around, pick a blocker. Our app is coming soon to iOS and isn't available to download yet. Join the launch newsletter to hear when it is. For a wider look at calming tools, see our comparison of [apps for nervous system regulation](/blog/best-apps-nervous-system-regulation/).

## FAQ
**Is there a screen time app that doesn't block apps completely?**
Yes. one sec delays apps instead of blocking them, ScreenZen adds delays you can always get past, Inscreen sends awareness prompts, and Jomo pairs schedules with mindful breaks. You can also dismiss Apple's Screen Time limits by default. Most of these apps include optional strict modes, so whether an app works as a blocker depends on the settings you choose. Start with the gentlest setup and tighten it only if you need to.

**Is ScreenZen really free?**
Yes. ScreenZen's App Store listing shows it as free, and its only in-app purchases are optional tips of $5, $10, $20 or $40 (USD, checked October 27, 2026). The free app includes the delays, breathing during the wait and the scrolling check-ins. It also offers optional strict blocks and lock settings, so if you want it to stay gentle, leave those off when you set it up.

**Does one sec actually work, or do people just get used to it?**
Both happen. A six-week study of 280 people found that one sec cut app openings by 57%, though the study's authors include the app's developer. A longer study of 1,039 users found that people took breaks from the friction and quickly went back to heavy use. Friction seems to work best while it's switched on, so gentle settings you're willing to keep may matter more than strict ones you'll end up disabling.

**Why do I keep ignoring Screen Time limits, and is there a gentler option?**
By default, Screen Time's limit screen is easy to dismiss, and it only asks you for a tap, so dismissing it quickly becomes automatic. A gentler option that still gets through asks for something small: a breath (one sec, ScreenZen), a question about your intent (Inscreen), or a written intention (Opal's Breaks). Setting limits slightly above your usual use also helps the screen feel like information rather than a scolding.

**Can an app help me feel less wired after scrolling, rather than just scroll less?**
Most screen time apps measure success in opens and minutes, and the published studies of friction apps measured phone use, not mood. Research links slow breathing to more relaxation and lower arousal, so a pause built around a minute of longer exhales may help you feel calmer. You don't need an app for that: put the phone face down and breathe in for 4 counts and out for 6, five or six times.

**Do breathing exercises in screen time apps do anything?**
In apps like one sec and ScreenZen, the breathing works mainly as a delay: a few seconds that interrupt the automatic urge to open the app. We found no studies of their breathing animations specifically. A small body of research links breathing slower than 10 breaths per minute to more relaxation, but those studies tested longer practice than a single breath when an app opens. Treat the in-app breath as a speed bump, and add a minute of slow breathing when you want to actually calm down.

# How to Stop Doomscrolling Without Quitting Your Phone

URL: https://derot.org/blog/how-to-stop-doomscrolling/
Updated: 2026-10-26

Key takeaways:
- Doomscrolling is continuing to scroll through negative or distressing content after it has started to make you feel worse. The signal is how you feel, not how long you've been scrolling.
- Feeds pull you toward bad news: in a study of about 105,000 headline variations tested in randomized experiments, each extra negative word raised click-through by about 2.3%.
- The most useful moment to act is mid-scroll. Notice a tight jaw or shallow breath, pause, breathe in for 4 and out for 6 for about 30 seconds, then choose on purpose.
- Most research linking doomscrolling to lower well-being is correlational, and the main study of a pause app was coauthored by the app's creator. The evidence is promising but not settled.
- You don't have to quit. In a 154-person trial, a one-week break from four platforms improved well-being, and targeted breaks are a gentler option worth trying.

To stop doomscrolling, interrupt it instead of trying to forbid it. When you notice the wired feeling (tight jaw, raised shoulders, shallow breath), take your thumb off the screen and breathe slowly for about 30 seconds with a longer exhale (in for 4, out for 6). One to three physiological sighs also work. Then decide on purpose whether to keep scrolling.

That's the whole method. The rest of this page covers why it tends to work better than the usual advice and what the research does and doesn't show. It also gives you scripts for the next time you come up from the news with your shoulders up by your ears.

Most guides on how to stop doomscrolling tell you to set limits, delete apps and rely on willpower. Those can help some people. But they aim at minutes, and the real problem is a state: the point where the feed has wound you up and you keep going anyway. A ban asks you to never reach that point. A short reset meets you once you're already there, which is when you actually need help.

## What is doomscrolling? The meaning in one sentence

Doomscrolling is continuing to scroll through negative or distressing content after it has started to make you feel worse. What defines it isn't the content alone or the time spent. It's the gap between how you feel and what you keep doing.

So the line between doomscrolling and ordinary scrolling is how you feel, not how many minutes have passed. Twenty minutes of friends' holiday photos and cooking videos usually isn't doomscrolling. Four minutes refreshing a disaster thread while your jaw tightens is.

Researchers now measure it, so it's more than a buzzword. Psychologists have developed a [validated Doomscrolling Scale in 15-item and 4-item versions](https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/ariqol/v18y2023i2d10.1007_s11482-022-10110-7.html), and a [2025 study of 300 Italian adults validated both versions](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-025-07976-9) in another language and culture.

## Why is it so hard to stop doomscrolling?

Three things make it hard. Feeds are full of content that grabs a nervous system on alert. Uncertainty makes you keep checking for the update that will finally settle things. And infinite feeds have no natural place to stop. None of this is a character flaw.

### Negative content gets more clicks

A large study of news headlines analyzed [about 105,000 headline variations tested in randomized experiments and roughly 5.7 million clicks. For an average-length headline, each additional negative word raised click-through by about 2.3%](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10202797/). Positive words lowered clicks, and [sad words were more effective than angry or scary ones](https://www.niemanlab.org/2023/03/negative-words-in-news-headlines-generate-more-clicks-but-sad-words-are-more-effective-than-angry-or-scary-ones/). The study looked at news headlines, not your social feed specifically, but the pattern is clear: whatever gets clicked tends to get made and shown again.

### Uncertainty keeps you checking

When a story is still unfolding, checking feels like it should help. Often it doesn't. Researchers who study problematic news consumption describe a [vicious cycle: people check more to relieve their distress, and the checking feeds the distress](https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/08/24/news-addiction-linked-to-poor-mental-physical-health-study). Each refresh promises resolution, and most deliver another fragment.

### The feed has no bottom

A newspaper ends. A broadcast ends. Infinite scroll and autoplay remove those built-in stopping points, so the decision to stop has to come from you, usually when you're least settled enough to make it. (To be fair to the feed, it has never once run out of things to worry about.)

So the problem is the feed, not you. That's also why "just use more willpower" tends to fail. It asks the most wound-up version of you to make the calmest decision of the day.

## Is doomscrolling bad for your mental health? What the evidence shows

Doomscrolling is associated with higher distress and lower well-being. But the research so far is mostly correlational, so it can't show that doomscrolling causes those outcomes.

- In a [study of 460 people, doomscrolling was linked to lower life satisfaction and mental well-being, and psychological distress explained the link](https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/ariqol/v18y2023i2d10.1007_s11482-022-10110-7.html). The data came from a single point in time and was self-reported.
- In a [survey of 1,100 US adults, 16.5% showed severely problematic news consumption, and 73.6% of that group reported mental ill-being, compared with 8% of the other participants](https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/08/24/news-addiction-linked-to-poor-mental-physical-health-study). Another [27.3% were moderately affected, 27.5% minimally, and 28.7% not at all](https://www.scimex.org/newsfeed/doomscrolling-linked-to-poor-mental-and-physical-health).
- The Italian validation study notes that [research associates doomscrolling with lower quality of life and poorer well-being](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-025-07976-9).

The honest reading is that these studies show a connection, not a direction. Stressful news may wear people down, and people who are already struggling may check more. Probably both are true. You don't need a causal study to notice that you feel worse after twenty minutes of bad news, though. That feeling is reason enough to do something about it.

## How to stop doomscrolling in the moment: a 4-step mid-scroll reset

The most useful time to act is mid-scroll, after the feed has wound you up. Not hours later, and not in a resolution you make on Sunday. These four steps take under a minute.

### 1. Notice the cues

Your body usually knows before you do. Common signs:

- A tight or clenched jaw
- Shoulders creeping up toward your ears
- Shallow, high breathing, or realizing you've been holding your breath
- Rereading the same bad news, or refreshing a page you just refreshed
- A low hum of dread that wasn't there when you picked up the phone

You don't need all of them. Any one of them is your cue.

### 2. Pause mid-scroll

Take your thumb off the screen and look up. Rest your eyes on something farther away, like a window, a wall or across the room. You're not closing the app or making a rule. You're just making a gap.

### 3. Reset for about 30 seconds

Pick one of these:

- **Longer-exhale breathing (4-6):** breathe in through your nose for 4 counts, then out slowly through your nose or soft lips for 6 counts. Three breaths take about 30 seconds. Keep it gentle and unforced, as if you're letting the air go rather than pushing it out. Our [step-by-step guide to 4-6 breathing](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/) covers the details, and the [free calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) paces it for you.
- **Physiological sigh:** take a full breath in through your nose, add a short second sip of air on top, then let it out in a long, slow exhale through your mouth. One to three sighs is plenty mid-scroll. The [physiological sigh timer](/tools/physiological-sigh/) walks you through it.

You may notice your shoulders drop by the second or third exhale. If your phone often leaves you feeling wired, our piece on [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/) explains what's happening in your body and how to come down.

**A quick safety note:** stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, lightheaded, tingly or short of breath. Don't over-breathe, and don't keep sighing back to back, which can make you lightheaded. Breathing can help you feel calmer, but it isn't a treatment for anxiety or any other condition.

### 4. Choose on purpose

Now ask yourself one question: do I want more of this right now? Then pick one of three options:

1. Keep going, knowing that you chose to.
2. Switch to something that doesn't wind you up.
3. Close the app.

Any of the three is fine. What matters is that it's a choice and not momentum.

### What the evidence says about pausing and breathing

Two lines of research back this sequence, and both have real limits.

**On pausing:** researchers studied the app one sec, which shows a pop-up before a chosen app opens. In the [field study, published in PNAS](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9974409), they followed 280 iOS users for six weeks. Users dismissed 36% of their attempts to open a target app after the pop-up, and actual openings fell 57%. A [separate controlled experiment with 500 people](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9974409) found that the most effective ingredient was simply having a real option to dismiss. A 10-second delay added nothing beyond that, and a generic message on its own didn't work. The caveats matter: the field study had no control group, users chose to take part, and one of the coauthors created the app. Still, the findings fit the idea that a pause plus a real choice does more than a timer or a warning.

**On breathing:** a [remote randomized trial with 108 participants](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/) found that five minutes a day of cyclic sighing for 28 days improved positive mood more than mindfulness meditation did (1.89 vs 1.22) and lowered breathing rate more. All groups improved, though. The study was exploratory, practice was self-reported and couldn't be closely verified, and it found no significant change in heart rate variability. It also excluded people with heart disease, seizures, pregnancy or psychosis. And it tested a daily five-minute practice, not a 30-second reset. So treat it as encouraging, not as proof of what a single mid-scroll sigh does.

That mid-scroll moment is the one we built DeRot for. It pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths, so the wired feeling can fade before you decide what to do next. DeRot is coming soon to iOS. Until then, the free timers above guide the same breathing.

## 60-second scripts for common doomscrolling moments

Save these, or just remember the one that fits you best.

### "Ten minutes into bad news, jaw tight"

- **0 to 5 seconds:** thumb off the screen, eyes up.
- **5 to 35 seconds:** three breaths, in for 4 and out for 6. Let your jaw unclench on each exhale.
- **35 to 50 seconds:** ask yourself, "Do I need more of this right now?"
- **50 to 60 seconds:** act on the answer. Close the app, switch to something else, or keep going on purpose.

### "Refreshing for updates on a developing story"

- **0 to 20 seconds:** one or two physiological sighs.
- **20 to 40 seconds:** pick one later time to check in (say, 6 p.m.) and one source you trust.
- **40 to 60 seconds:** close the tab. Most developing stories make more sense after a few hours than after a few refreshes.

### "In bed, can't put it down"

- **0 to 10 seconds:** turn the phone face down on the bed or nightstand.
- **10 to 60 seconds:** five slow breaths, in for 4 and out for 6. If that feels easy, let the exhale stretch a little longer, without forcing it.
- **After:** leave the phone face down. If this happens most nights, our guide to [doomscrolling at night](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/) explains why late scrolling feels so wired and how to come down before sleep.

## What is mindful scrolling?

Mindful scrolling means using social apps while staying aware of how they're making you feel, and acting on what you notice. It doesn't mean scrolling less on principle. It means catching the shift from "this is interesting" to "this is making me tense" and treating that shift as your cue to pause. The four-step reset above is mindful scrolling with a concrete way out.

## Common mistakes when trying to stop doomscrolling

- **All-or-nothing rules.** "No news after 7 p.m., ever" sounds great until a big story breaks or you have a bad day, and then the whole rule collapses. A reset you can do every time beats a rule you keep for nine days.
- **Deleting apps you'll reinstall within a week.** Deleting makes sense for an app you genuinely don't want. But if you need an app for friends, work or your community, it usually comes back, and you're back where you started.
- **Saying "just one more" right after the reset.** The reset works by giving you a choice. If the choice keeps being "one more," make step 4 physical: set the phone down for one more breath before you decide.
- **Using breath holds or fast breathing when you're already wired.** Techniques like 4-7-8, box breathing or rapid breathing have their place, but they aren't for everyone. That includes people who are pregnant, have heart or lung conditions, or have a history of fainting or panic. Mid-scroll, stick to gentle longer exhales.
- **Treating it as a failure of willpower.** You're up against feeds designed to hold your attention. Blaming yourself just stacks a second layer of stress on top of the first.

## How to take a break from social media without quitting

You don't have to quit to get some of the benefits of a break. Targeted breaks, from one platform or at certain hours, are a reasonable middle ground. The strongest evidence so far, though, comes from a full week off.

In a [randomized trial of 154 adults](https://researchportal.bath.ac.uk/en/publications/taking-a-one-week-break-from-social-media-improves-well-being-dep/), a one-week break from Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and TikTok improved well-being, depression and anxiety scores compared with usual use. Well-being rose 4.9 points, depression fell 2.2 and anxiety fell 1.7. Less time on the apps partly explained the improvements, and the drop in anxiety was linked specifically to less time on TikTok. That hints that the platform that winds you up most may matter more than your total time. But it wasn't a clinical sample, the follow-up lasted one week, and the study tested a full break. It doesn't prove that smaller breaks work the same way.

Practical options that don't involve deleting anything:

- **A news-free evening** once or twice a week.
- **Mute one source** that reliably leaves you feeling worse, instead of overhauling your whole feed.
- **Unfollow outrage accounts**, even ones you agree with.
- **Keep one daily news window**, using one or two sources you trust.
- **Pause one platform** for a week, starting with whichever app leaves you most wired.

## When to talk to someone

Talk to a doctor or mental health professional if checking the news keeps feeding your worry, if it's getting in the way of your sleep, work or relationships, or if the distress stays even when the phone is away. Breathing and pauses can help you feel calmer in the moment, but they don't replace real support.

If you're in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency services. In the US, you can call or text 988.

## FAQ
**What's the difference between doomscrolling and regular scrolling?**
The difference is how you feel, not how long you scroll. Regular scrolling can be relaxing or useful, and you can put the phone down easily. Doomscrolling is continuing to scroll through negative or distressing content after it has already started making you feel worse: jaw tight, breath shallow, rereading the same bad news. Twenty pleasant minutes may be fine, while five tense minutes on a disaster thread is a good cue to pause.

**Do app blockers or screen-time limits work for doomscrolling?**
They help some people, especially those who want a firm boundary. A study of the friction app one sec found that a pop-up with a real option to dismiss cut app openings, and that a simple delay added little beyond that choice. One of the coauthors created the app, though. Limits target minutes, but doomscrolling is about how you feel. That's why many people do better pairing any limit with a short breathing reset at the moment the feed winds them up.

**Why do I doomscroll at night?**
At night you're tired, fewer things interrupt you, and the phone is often the last thing between you and a quiet room, so nothing gives you a natural place to stop. Stressful news can also leave you feeling wired right when you want to wind down. Turning the phone face down and taking a few slow breaths with a longer exhale can help you come back down before you try to sleep.

**What is mindful scrolling?**
Mindful scrolling is using social apps while paying attention to how they make you feel, and acting on what you notice. It doesn't mean scrolling less on principle. It means noticing when the feed shifts from interesting to tense, then pausing, taking a few slow breaths and choosing whether to keep going. Many people find this easier to stick with than strict limits, because it works with the apps they actually want to keep.

**Does taking a week off social media actually help?**
It can. In a 2022 randomized trial of 154 adults, a one-week break from Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and TikTok improved well-being, depression and anxiety scores compared with normal use. The drop in anxiety was linked to less time on TikTok. It was a short study that wasn't tested in clinical populations, so a full week off is one option, not a requirement. Taking a break from just the platform that winds you up most is a gentler place to start.

## Sources
- Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal (Balban et al.): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/
- Directing smartphone use through the self-nudge app one sec (Grüning, Riedel, Lorenz-Spreen): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9974409
- Negativity drives online news consumption (Robertson et al.): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10202797/
- Negative words in news headlines generate more clicks, but sad words are more effective than angry or scary ones: https://www.niemanlab.org/2023/03/negative-words-in-news-headlines-generate-more-clicks-but-sad-words-are-more-effective-than-angry-or-scary-ones/
- Doomscrolling Scale: its association with personality traits, psychological distress, social media use, and wellbeing (Satici et al.): https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/ariqol/v18y2023i2d10.1007_s11482-022-10110-7.html
- Italian validation of the Doomscrolling Scale: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-025-07976-9

# How Long Should You Do Box Breathing For? From 1 Minute to 5

URL: https://derot.org/blog/how-long-to-do-box-breathing/
Updated: 2026-10-23

Key takeaways:
- One round of 4-4-4-4 box breathing takes 16 seconds, so four rounds is about one minute and five minutes is about 18 to 19 rounds.
- In a 2026 preregistered pilot of 47 students, one minute of box breathing during real anxious moments reduced state anxiety more than a passive control, measured five minutes later.
- In the 2023 Stanford trial of 5 minutes a day for 28 days, mood gains across the breathing groups grew with the number of days practiced, but box breathing did not significantly beat mindfulness and HRV did not change.
- You can stop once your breath slows on its own and your shoulders drop. More minutes are not automatically better.
- If 4-second holds feel like too much, switch to 3-3-3-3 or 2-2-2-2, or skip the hold after the exhale. Stop if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.

How long should you do box breathing for? For a quick reset, four rounds of 4-4-4-4 is enough, and that takes about one minute. For a fuller reset, aim for about five minutes. As a habit, [once or twice a day](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/box-breathing-benefits) is a common recommendation. Short sessions count.

Most guides bury a single number ("a few minutes," "three to four rounds") somewhere near the bottom. The more useful answer depends on why you're doing it, so below we break it down by situation, then cover the research and how to tell when you can stop.

## The quick math: how long one round of box breathing takes

Box breathing is a paced breathing technique: you breathe in for a count of four, hold for four, breathe out for four and hold again for four, tracing the four sides of a box. One trip around the box is one round.

At one second per count, one round takes 16 seconds. That makes the numbers simple:

- 4 rounds: about 64 seconds
- 8 rounds: about 2 minutes
- 18 to 19 rounds: about 5 minutes

If you'd rather not count, the [free box breathing timer](/tools/box-breathing-timer/) paces the 4-4-4-4 pattern for you. Stop after four rounds for a one-minute reset, or let it run for about five minutes for a longer session.

## How many rounds of box breathing should you do?

Four rounds is the most common answer, and it's a good default for calming down in the moment. [Cleveland Clinic suggests three to four rounds](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/box-breathing-benefits), and both [University of Minnesota Extension](https://extension.umn.edu/community/community-development/economy-and-development/vital-connections/two-for-you-video-series/box-breathing) and [RWJBarnabas Health](https://www.rwjbh.org/documents/institute-for-prevention/How-to-Practice-Box-Breathing.pdf) suggest four. A [University of Michigan handout](https://mari.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/MARI-FY26-Box_Breathing_Handout.pdf) goes a bit longer, suggesting at least five boxes, and says you can start with a count of 2 or 3.

| Situation | Rounds (4-4-4-4) | Time | What it's for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mid-scroll reset | 4 | About 1 minute | Taking the edge off after a feed has wound you up |
| Fuller reset | 18 to 19 | About 5 minutes | When one minute took the edge off but you want to settle further |
| Daily practice | 4 to 19 | 1 to 5 minutes, once or twice a day | Making the technique familiar so it's easy to reach for |
| Winding down at night | 4 to 8, with gentler counts | 1 to 2 minutes | A quiet transition toward bed |

These sources don't really disagree. Three or four rounds is sized for a single stressful moment, and five or more minutes is closer to a practice session. None of these numbers come from a trial that compared different lengths of box breathing, so treat them as sensible starting points rather than prescribed doses.

## Is 1 minute of box breathing enough?

For taking the edge off a stressful moment, one minute may well be enough. In a [2026 preregistered pilot study of 47 students](https://edoc.ku.de/id/eprint/36573/1/Simply%20breathing%20anxiety%20away%20A%20pilot%20just-in-time%20ecological%20momentary%20intervention%20study%20of%20one-minute%20cyclic%20sighing%20versus%20box%20breathing%20as%20tool.pdf), one minute of box breathing during real anxious moments in daily life reduced state anxiety more than a passive control, measured five minutes later. One minute of cyclic sighing did too.

Keep that result in proportion, though. It's a small pilot study in students, and what we can report comes from the study's abstract. It suggests a short session can help in the moment. It doesn't show that one minute is the ideal length, or that it works for everyone.

The same study also found [slower reaction times after both breathing exercises](https://edoc.ku.de/id/eprint/36573/1/Simply%20breathing%20anxiety%20away%20A%20pilot%20just-in-time%20ecological%20momentary%20intervention%20study%20of%20one-minute%20cyclic%20sighing%20versus%20box%20breathing%20as%20tool.pdf). The authors called this unexpected, and box breathing was also linked to fewer inhibition errors, especially in participants with higher trait anxiety. Either way, it's sensible to give yourself a short pause before anything that needs quick reactions, such as driving.

## Box breathing mid-scroll: a 60-second script

Here's the moment we have in mind. You picked up your phone to check one thing. Twenty minutes later your jaw is tight, your shoulders are up near your ears, and you feel oddly wired for someone who has been sitting still. That's the feed doing what feeds do, and it's a good time for four rounds. (We explain why it happens in [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/).)

1. Put the phone face down, or turn the screen off.
2. Breathe out fully so you start the box empty.
3. Breathe in gently through your nose for 4.
4. Hold for 4, keeping your throat and shoulders soft rather than clamped.
5. Breathe out slowly for 4.
6. Hold, empty, for 4.
7. Repeat for four rounds. Tap one finger against your thumb at the end of each round so you don't have to keep count in your head.
8. Let your breathing go back to normal for a couple of breaths and notice how you feel.

That's it. You can stop at four rounds. If you'd like something to follow, open the [box breathing timer](/tools/box-breathing-timer/) and stop it after about a minute.

DeRot is built for this mid-scroll moment. It pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths, so the wired feeling can fade before you go back to the feed. It's coming soon to iOS.

## What does a 5-minute session do? What the Stanford study found

The best-known study of box breathing used five-minute sessions: a [2023 Stanford randomized trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) in which 108 people spent five minutes a day for 28 days on mindfulness meditation or on one of several breathing practices, including box breathing and cyclic sighing. Twenty-one people were assigned to box breathing.

Here's what it found:

- Positive mood went up in the box breathing group, but [only cyclic sighing significantly beat mindfulness](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) on positive mood.
- State anxiety fell in every group, including mindfulness, with no significant differences between groups.
- Across the breathing groups as a whole, gains in positive mood grew with the number of days people practiced. The paper doesn't report this for box breathing on its own.
- There was [no significant change in heart rate variability (HRV) or resting heart rate](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947).

On HRV, the broader picture is more encouraging. A [2022 review of 223 studies](https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38169/) found that slow breathing in general increased vagally mediated HRV during sessions, right after them, and over multiple sessions. That hasn't been shown for box breathing specifically, so we wouldn't promise it.

The Stanford study was exploratory, and each technique had a small group. Its results suggest that five minutes of daily box breathing may lift mood and ease anxiety without clearly beating mindfulness meditation, and that across the breathing groups, practicing on more days went with bigger mood gains. That's a long way from headlines about a [five-minute breathing trick to "kill stress instantly"](https://gearpatrol.com/2020/02/18/box-breathing-navy-seals/). The evidence describes a modest, gentle effect, not an off switch.

## How do you know when you can stop?

You can stop once the edge is gone, even if that's before your planned number of rounds. We haven't found research that pins down a stopping point for box breathing, so these cues come from experience rather than studies:

- Your breath starts to slow and deepen on its own, and the counts feel easy rather than effortful.
- Your jaw unclenches and your shoulders drop.
- The urge to keep counting fades, and you can think about what's next without a jolt.

If you've done four rounds and still feel wound up, do four more, or switch to a pattern with a longer exhale. Beyond that, more minutes aren't automatically better. Box breathing is a way back to baseline, not an endurance event.

## What if 4-second holds feel like too much?

Shorten the counts. Box breathing works at whatever length lets you breathe without strain. Four seconds is a convention, not a rule.

- **3-3-3-3:** 12-second rounds, five rounds a minute.
- **2-2-2-2:** 8-second rounds, a good place to start if holds make you uneasy.
- **Skip the empty hold:** breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, then go straight into the next inhale. Many people find the hold after the exhale the hardest part.

This matches both the research and the clinical advice. In the Stanford trial, [box counts were personalized, from about 3 to 4 seconds up to 8 to 10 seconds, and participants were told to shorten them if they felt strained](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947). Cleveland Clinic says to [breathe gently, without straining](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/box-breathing-benefits), and notes that the counts can lengthen with practice. You can lengthen them over time if you enjoy it, but you don't have to.

If holds don't suit you at all, try [calm 4-6 breathing](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/): in for 4, out for 6, with no holds. Our [guide to 4-6 breathing](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/) walks you through it. For a 3-3-3-3 or 2-2-2-2 box, the [custom breathing timer](/tools/custom-breathing-timer/) lets you set your own pattern.

## How often should you do box breathing?

Once or twice a day is a reasonable rhythm, plus any time you need it. [Cleveland Clinic recommends one or two times a day](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/box-breathing-benefits) regardless of how you feel, which keeps the technique familiar for when you need it.

The Stanford data also shows what a realistic habit looks like. [Breathwork participants averaged 5.76 minutes a day on 19.6 of the 28 days](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947). They missed some days, and their mood gains still grew with the number of days they practiced. So a few minutes on most days is a realistic target. The study didn't compare that with occasional longer sessions.

At bedtime, keep it gentle: shorter counts, a dim room, and a few minutes at most. Some people find the holds a little alerting at night and prefer a longer exhale instead. If scrolling is what keeps you up, [doomscrolling at night](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/) covers that side of it. If you have ongoing trouble sleeping, talk to a doctor.

## When to stop: dizziness and other safety notes

Box breathing is gentle for most people, but a few rules matter.

- **Stop if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.** Go back to normal breathing and sit or lie down. Next time, shorten the counts or skip the hold after the exhale.
- **Keep it slow and soft.** Don't force your breath or speed up the pattern.
- **Check with a clinician first** if you're pregnant or have a heart or lung condition, seizures, glaucoma, a history of fainting, or panic that gets worse when you focus on your breathing.
- **Never hold your breath in or near water, or while driving.**
- **Pause before tasks that need quick reactions**, since [reaction times may be slower right after a session](https://edoc.ku.de/id/eprint/36573/1/Simply%20breathing%20anxiety%20away%20A%20pilot%20just-in-time%20ecological%20momentary%20intervention%20study%20of%20one-minute%20cyclic%20sighing%20versus%20box%20breathing%20as%20tool.pdf).
- **It isn't a treatment.** Box breathing can help you feel calmer, but it doesn't treat anxiety, panic or insomnia. If stress or anxiety is persistent or getting in the way of your life, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US, or contact your local emergency services.

## FAQ
**How fast does box breathing work?**
Many people notice a small shift within a minute or two: their breath slows and their shoulders loosen. In a 2026 pilot study of 47 students, one minute of box breathing during anxious moments reduced state anxiety more than a passive control, measured five minutes later. It's a small study, so treat it as encouraging rather than proof. In the 2023 Stanford trial, mood gains across the breathing groups grew with the number of days people practiced over four weeks.

**Can you do box breathing for too long, and why do I feel dizzy?**
There's no set maximum, but longer isn't automatically better, and long holds or forceful breathing can leave some people dizzy or lightheaded. That usually means the counts are too long or you're breathing too hard. Stop, breathe normally and sit down. Next time, try 3-3-3-3 or 2-2-2-2, or skip the hold after the exhale. If the dizziness keeps happening, check with a clinician.

**Does box breathing raise HRV?**
Not clearly. In the 2023 Stanford trial, five minutes a day for 28 days led to no significant change in heart rate variability or resting heart rate. A 2022 review of 223 studies found that slow breathing in general increases vagally mediated HRV during and after sessions, but that hasn't been shown for box breathing specifically. The more consistent findings are about mood and feeling calmer.

**Is box breathing better than cyclic sighing or 4-7-8?**
No technique is clearly best for everyone. In the Stanford trial, cyclic sighing was the only practice that significantly beat mindfulness on positive mood, and box breathing did not. In a 2026 pilot, one minute of either box breathing or cyclic sighing reduced anxiety more than doing nothing. 4-7-8 uses a longer hold and a longer exhale. Pick the one that feels comfortable and that you'll actually use.

**Is box breathing good before sleep?**
It can be a calm way to wind down, but there's no strong evidence that it treats sleep problems. At night, keep the counts short and gentle and stop after a few minutes. Some people find the holds a little alerting and prefer a pattern with a longer exhale, such as breathing in for 4 and out for 6. If you have ongoing trouble sleeping, talk to a doctor.

**Should I lengthen the count over time?**
Only if you want to. Cleveland Clinic notes that the counts can lengthen with practice, and in the Stanford trial counts were personalized, ranging from 3 to 4 seconds up to 8 to 10 seconds. But longer isn't better by default. The right count is the one you can keep up without straining, gasping or feeling lightheaded. Plenty of people stay at a count of 4, or 3, indefinitely.

- Effects of voluntary slow breathing on heart rate and heart rate variability (Laborde et al.): https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38169/
